sections.text:
It is a note of thirteen verses. It comes from one who calls himself only the elder, and it is addressed to the chosen lady and her children, whom he loves in truth. He is glad. He has found some of her children “walking in truth”.

What he asks for is not new. It is the old command, the one they have had from the beginning, “that we love one another.” And love, he says, means walking according to God’s commandments.

Then the tone sharpens. Many deceivers have gone out into the world who do not confess that Jesus Christ came in the flesh. He tells his readers to guard what they have gained, and not to give such teachers a welcome. If anyone comes who does not bring this teaching, “don’t receive him into your house, and don’t welcome him”.

The elder would rather say more face to face than with paper and ink.

The chosen lady is most often understood as a local church and her children as its members, though some take her to be an individual woman. Tradition identifies the elder with the apostle John. In the first century traveling teachers depended on the hospitality of believers.

The instruction not to welcome false teachers is about lending support to their teaching, and readers generally do not take it as a ban on ordinary kindness or conversation. The letter holds truth and love together and will not let either stand without the other. Truth without love becomes hard, and love without truth loses its direction, and so the short note asks for both.

A short note with a warm start. The elder writes to the chosen lady and her children, whom he loves in truth, and not he only but all who know the truth. Some take the lady to be a woman and her household, others a congregation.

His joy is plain: he has found some of her children walking in truth. And his request is small but large. Let us love one another. This is love, that we walk according to his commandments, and that is the commandment you heard from the beginning.

Then a warning. Many deceivers have gone out into the world, those who do not confess that Jesus Christ came in the flesh. Watch yourselves. Anyone who does not remain in the teaching of Christ does not have God.

Verses 10 and 11 tell the readers not to receive such a person into the house. Read in their setting, they concern traveling teachers who spread this teaching, not a general rule of hostility.

The elder has more to say but hopes to come and speak “face to face”.

The writer calls himself only the elder. Tradition links this note to the apostle John, and its language and themes are close to those of 1 John, so many scholars think the same person or circle wrote them. In the first Christian centuries, traveling teachers depended on the hospitality of local believers, and that is the setting for the warning in verses 10 and 11.
